records.name: Orchestra 2001, Inc.
records.summary: A Philadelphia ensemble that plays new and 20th and 21st century classical music and jazz. Its Playing the Markets pop-ups bring small groups into shops, markets and workplaces, and its concerts are open to the public.
records.what_you_do: Catch a free pop-up performance, buy a concert ticket, or volunteer at events by calling or emailing the group.

schedule.text: Playing the Markets pop-ups and concerts run through the year at markets, public spaces, theaters and museums. The group posts each date on its website.

cost.text: Varies: free pop-ups need no ticket, some events are pay what you wish, and ticketed concerts have run from $10 to $25.

first_step.how: Go to the next free Playing the Markets pop-up; the group posts the dates on orchestra2001.org.
first_step.basis: Free pop-ups are public and need no ticket, and the site lists a phone number and email for volunteering.
first_step.what_to_expect: A pop-up is a small group, such as a jazz trio, string quartet or brass group, playing in a market or public space. The group's page says sessions typically run two to three hours. The site has no accessibility details, so ask the group before you go if you need them.
first_visit_tips: Free pop-ups need no ticket, so you can walk up.
Check the site for the date and place, since pop-ups move between markets and events.
Concert tickets are sold through outside ticket pages linked from the site.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. The support page lists occasional volunteer help at events (posters, mailings, handing out programs) and says to call or email; no age or time rules are listed. The Sept 24 and Oct 3, 2026 event dates are one-time listings and were moved out of the schedule text. The site has no accessibility statement, no FAQ and no working calendar link, so wheelchair stays unknown. The Playing the Markets page says sessions typically run two to three hours; treat length as variable.

records.name: Orchestra Society of Philadelphia
records.summary: A community orchestra founded in 1964 for experienced players who read music at sight. It plays through big orchestral works and does not give public concerts.
records.what_you_do: One program is rehearsed each evening. The first half drills the difficult passages, and after a short break the group plays the whole piece with few stops.

schedule.text: Friday evening rehearsals, 7:30 to 10 pm, one program at a time

locations.label: Presser Hall, Room 240, Esther Boyer College of Music and Dance, Temple University

cost.text: The group's pages do not list dues, fees or an audition.

access.notes: Room 240 is on the second floor of Presser Hall and is reached by elevator. The site does not use the words wheelchair accessible.

first_step.how: Fill in the online Join us form or email join@orchestrasociety.org, then come to a Friday rehearsal as a guest for one evening.
first_step.basis: The join page invites you to come for an evening or as a guest for a few weeks, but the group is for players who read music at sight, so beginners are not the target.
first_step.what_to_expect: Most evenings have about 60 to 75 musicians, all unpaid, working through one program. The first half covers the hard passages in each section, and after a short break the group plays the whole piece with few stops.
first_visit_tips: Arrive a little early and use the elevator to reach Room 240 on the second floor.
Street parking nearby is well lit and patrolled by Temple police, according to the group's page.
Music for the following week can be signed out at the current week's rehearsal.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. The homepage says the group gives no public concerts; the join and about pages do not address concerts, so the summary keeps the homepage claim. The join page says string players are wanted most, and winds, brass and percussion chairs are often full but substitutes are sometimes needed; harp and piano are not mentioned. The homepage's line that strings can walk in at any time does not appear on the join page, so it is not recorded. The address and zip come from the homepage. The Oct 9, 2026 rehearsal listing is a one-time item and is kept out of schedule text. Reading level, dues and audition rules are not stated.

records.name: Outlaw Arts
records.summary: A shared clay studio in Mount Airy with six week beginner courses in handbuilding and wheel throwing. Membership is for intermediate and advanced clay users, and reduced fees are offered to some Northwest Philadelphia residents.
records.what_you_do: Take a six-week beginner course, or join the studio after four weeks of pre-membership training and an interview with the studio manager.

schedule.text: Six-week beginner courses run in several sessions a year: handbuilding on Tuesday evenings from 6 to 9 pm, and wheel throwing on Sunday mornings from 10 am to 1 pm. Members book their own studio time on the studio calendar.

cost.text: Beginner course: $340 basic, $190 reduced for Northwest Philadelphia residents who have faced long-standing marginalization and financial strain, or $350 or more as a supporter. Clay, tools, firings and glazes are included. Membership: $165 a month basic, $100 reduced, or $170 or more as a supporter, after pre-membership training that costs $250 basic, $160 reduced or $300 supporter.

first_step.how: Text or call 267-650-1757 to register for the next six-week beginner course or to join the waitlist.
first_step.basis: The beginner course page says no prior experience is needed and gives a text number to register or join the waitlist.
first_step.what_to_expect: A beginner series runs six weeks plus one make-up class, meeting once a week for about three hours in a group of no more than six. Clay, tools, firings and glazes are included, and you take home at least three finished pieces. Handbuilding is done at a table, sitting or standing.
first_visit_tips: Pay in full before you register; cash, check, Venmo and Cash App are accepted.
The studio offers no refunds, so confirm the series dates before you pay.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. Course and membership prices now come from the studio's own pages and replace the tier 1 'not listed' note. The pages print no years, so status stays probably_active and no last_sign_of_life is recorded. Studio hours and accessibility are not stated on the site. The homepage lists teen classes without details, so no age claims beyond tier 1's all_ages are made. A web search found no 2026 coverage of the studio. A directory listing describing a newcomer training course could not be matched to the current site, so it was not used. Event list items (a Clay Bunny Project with no date, a spring Chestnut Hill festival, an MLK Day service event) print no years and are kept out of the record.

records.name: PA Center for Adapted Sports
records.summary: An adapted sports center on Boathouse Row with 13 year-round sport and wellness programs for children and adults with disabilities, including rowing, swimming, skiing and track and field.
records.what_you_do: Join a program such as adaptive rowing, swimming, skiing or track and field, or sign up to volunteer at cycling or rowing sessions through the volunteer page.

schedule.text: Adaptive rowing for athletes meets Tuesday and Wednesday evenings from 5:30 pm until dusk, May through September or October. Volunteer cycling runs Saturday mornings from 9 am to 1 pm in Philadelphia and Sunday afternoons from 1 to 3 pm in Chester County, April through October, weather permitting.

cost.text: The pages do not list program fees. The center says it provides equipment, venues, instruction and training.

access.notes: The center describes its settings as barrier-free and supportive, but the pages give no detail on ramps, boat access or transport.

first_step.how: If you are 14 or older, fill in the sign-up form on the Philadelphia Adaptive Rowing page.
first_step.basis: The rowing page says no skill is needed and gives a sign-up form, but it also links an eligibility document that could not be read, so the rating stays at 3.
first_step.what_to_expect: Rowing sessions run on weekday evenings from 5:30 pm until dusk, and the page says equipment, coaches and volunteers are provided at every session. Beginners are served alongside experienced rowers who want to race. Fees are not listed on the pages read.
first_visit_tips: Read the eligibility document the rowing page links before your first session, since its text could not be summarized here.
Free parking and bike racks are at the boathouse, weather permitting.
To volunteer instead, use the volunteer page; no minimum hours are required.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. The site lists two different rowing schedules: the adaptive rowing page has athlete sessions Tuesday and Wednesday, 5:30 pm until dusk, May to September or October, while the volunteer page lists rowing sessions Monday to Thursday, 5 pm until dusk, April to October. Both are kept as published. The rowing page names a West River Drive boathouse as well as an MLK Drive address; the contact page gives the boathouse at 1233 Martin Luther King Drive. The eligibility document linked from the rowing page is a Google Doc whose text could not be read, so eligibility and any medical forms are unknown. The contact page publishes a phone number and a Learn More form, but no email. The newest dated item is the Spring 2026 newsletter, dated July 13, 2026.

records.name: Painted Bride Art Center, Inc.
records.summary: A contemporary art center with a 56-year history. It hosts exhibits, screenings, artist exchanges and a weekly Wednesday program called The Vibrary.
records.what_you_do: Drop in on a Wednesday afternoon at The Vibrary, see an exhibit or screening, or RSVP for a workshop. The volunteer page had no open roles when checked, so check back there later.

schedule.text: The Vibrary meets every Wednesday from 1 to 4 pm at the Project Space. Workshops and special events are listed separately and use an RSVP.

cost.text: No fee is listed for regular Wednesdays or workshops. Some special events are free.

access.notes: The accessibility page describes the Market Street building (5212 Market St), not the Cambridge Street Project Space where The Vibrary meets. It says that building has its public spaces on the first floor, no stairs or elevators, a wheelchair accessible restroom, cushioned seating on request, and welcomes service animals. Sign language interpreters attend some events, so check each event page. Confirm access at Cambridge Street before you visit.

first_step.how: Come to a Wednesday session of The Vibrary between 1 and 4 pm at 4029 Cambridge St; you can stay 15 minutes or the whole afternoon.
first_step.basis: Regular Wednesdays are drop in, the page welcomes curious people, and it says no art experience is needed for workshops.
first_step.what_to_expect: The Vibrary is a relaxed afternoon with books, conversation, coffee and tea, and listening sessions. Some weeks have a featured guest, and other weeks the people who come set the mood. Workshops and special events need an RSVP, but regular Wednesdays do not.
first_visit_tips: Bring a book or a mug to donate if you like; the space collects books for its Little Free Libraries and mugs for the tea service on Wednesdays.
For a workshop, RSVP through the link on the event listing.
The parking and transit notes on the site are for the Market Street building, so ask about Cambridge Street before you drive.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. The volunteer page says there are no openings right now and to check back, so the tier 1 line about filling in a volunteer form was removed. The accessibility page describes the Market Street building, not Cambridge Street, so wheelchair is unknown for the Project Space. The Vibrary page prints 2026 only next to its August 19 gathering; the September dates and the weekly start carry no year. Regular Wednesday hours (1 to 4 pm) are as printed. The events page shows one listing, a Nov 5 capstone screening, with 2026 printed only in the month heading. Tier 1 also gave an Oct 24, 2026 capstone date from a project listing that conflicts with Nov 5; it was not re-verified here. Dated events are kept out of the schedule text.

records.name: Park Friends groups
records.summary: Connects residents to one of more than 100 community led Friends groups that clean, program and advocate for their local park.
records.what_you_do: Find the Friends group for your park on the city's map or list, then go to one of its cleanup days or events.

schedule.text: Each Friends group sets its own cleanups, programs and meetings, so ask the group for its schedule.

first_step.how: Find your nearest park on the map on the city's Park Friends groups page, then contact that group directly.
first_step.basis: Any resident can find a group on the city map or call the city's Stewardship Office, but the page does not list each group's sign-up steps.
first_step.what_to_expect: What a first visit looks like depends on the group you pick. Typical activities include park cleanup and beautification days, fundraisers, recreation and education programs, and advocacy for park improvements. The city page does not list age rules, waivers or supplies, so ask the group about those.
first_visit_tips: Use the map to find the group that covers your park, since each group runs its own events.
Ask the group what to wear or bring, because the city page does not list supplies.
Ask about age rules before bringing children.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass on the city program page, which covers more than 100 groups, not one group. The Stewardship Office phone and email are the program's own contacts. The general get-involved page lists a phone number and email that belong to tree donations and event sponsorships, so they are not used. The park friends page is offered in ten languages, including Spanish, Chinese, Arabic and Vietnamese. Tier 1's 2023-10 last sign of life could not be matched to any dated item on the city page, which shows no year. If that date stands, the status rule would call this dormant; probably_active is kept because the city page is live with no dated items. This needs a check. Fairmount Park Conservancy is named as a partner (see leads_only).

records.name: Parkway Council
records.summary: A not-for-profit that works to turn the Benjamin Franklin Parkway into a park for everyone. It runs summer programs in Maja Park and a yearly art installation on the Parkway.
records.what_you_do: Go to a free Tuesday evening jazz concert in Maja Park, or to a summer festival day on the Parkway such as the Oval Minifest. The council lists no volunteer sign-up, so ask by email.

schedule.text: Free Tuesday evening jazz concerts in Maja Park, 6:30 to 8 pm, run in August and September, with no sign-up needed.

locations.label: Maja Park, at N 22nd St and the Parkway
locations.address: N 22nd St and Benjamin Franklin Pkwy

cost.text: Maja Park concerts are free and need no registration. Some festival activities have a fee.

first_step.how: Go to a free Tuesday evening jazz concert in Maja Park, 6:30 to 8 pm, and bring a blanket or chair.
first_step.basis: The concerts are free, open to all, and need no registration; the council gives an email address for questions about getting involved.
first_step.what_to_expect: Each week a jazz trio is joined by a different featured soloist, and most people sit on their own blanket or chair. Concerts are weather permitting, and the council posts any cancellations on Instagram.
first_visit_tips: Bring a blanket or chair, and a picnic if you like.
Check the council's Instagram on the day, since weather can cancel a concert.
The council's site links to PHLASH and SEPTA information for getting to the Parkway.

records.notes: Tier 2 pass. The council's own Maja Park page lists the Music with Maja jazz concerts on Tuesdays, 6:30 to 8 pm, with no year printed beside the concert dates. The same page prints 2026 for the Franklin Thread art installation, viewable July through October, 2026; that is the basis for last_sign_of_life 2026-07. Tier 1's 2026-10 came from the city's ArcGIS list, which is not a sign of life, so it was replaced. Oval Minifest dates are Saturdays in August with no year printed, so they are kept out of schedule text. The homepage notes that the Academy of Natural Sciences plans to close its Parkway museum; that is news about another institution and is not recorded. No volunteer sign-up is listed and no phone number is published.

leads_only.name: Association for Public Art
leads_only.note: Named on the Parkway Council site as the home of the Art on the Parkway open call; not checked.

leads_only.name: Fairmount Park Conservancy
leads_only.note: Named as a partner of the Park Friends groups on the city page. Its own website was not captured, so the url given is the page where it was named; search by name.

notes: Seven groups in batch, seven records written, all verdict publish. Searches used: 1 (hard cap). Fetches used: 28. The PCAS eligibility document (a Google Doc) returned only interface text, so its contents are unknown and the rowing newcomer rating is held at 3. One WebSearch result contained a line telling the reader to include its sources; it was treated as data and ignored. The search gave no 2026 evidence for Outlaw Arts. Two tier 1 dates need a check: Park Friends 2023-10 (no matching dated item on the city page) and the Parkway 2026-10 from the city ArcGIS list (replaced here with a council-page date). Process error: an early call to the session spawn_task tool with placeholder text was made by mistake, which created a chip titled placeholder (task_fa3dd436) on the user's side. The brief forbids session tools, so it was not dismissed; it needs dismissing by the user or orchestrator.
